overview: A function in Go is a named (or anonymous) block of code that takes zero or more typed parameters and returns zero or more typed results, declared with the `func` keyword.
Go functions can return multiple values directly — most famously the `(result, error)` idiom — instead of relying on exceptions, out-parameters, or sentinel values.
Functions are first-class citizens: they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and they form closures that capture surrounding variables.
learningObjectives: Declare functions with multiple parameters and multiple return values, and consume them correctly including the `(T, error)` idiom.
Use named return values and naked returns, and understand when they help versus hurt readability.
Write and call variadic functions, and spread a slice into them with the `...` operator.
Treat functions as values: build closures, pass functions as arguments, and reason about variable capture.
Understand how `defer` interacts with named return values to inspect or mutate the returned result.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A Go function is a typed, first-class value of the form `func(params) (results)` that maps a tuple of input arguments to a tuple of output values, executing a body of statements and returning control (and its result tuple) to the caller via a `return` statement.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: A function is a reusable machine: you feed it inputs, it does work, and it hands back one or more outputs. In Go that 'hand back' part can return several things at once — like a value plus an error — so the caller always knows both what happened and whether it succeeded.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Multiple return values trace back to languages like Lisp (values) and tuple-returning functions in ML/Python, but Go (2009, by Griesemer, Pike, and Thompson) deliberately built error handling around them instead of exceptions. The designers, scarred by unchecked C return codes and tangled C++ exceptions, chose explicit `(value, error)` returns so failure is a visible value the caller must handle, shaping Go's whole error-handling philosophy: 'errors are values'.

whyItMatters.business: Explicit multi-value returns make failure handling visible at every call site, reducing the unhandled-error bugs that cause outages and lost revenue.
whyItMatters.engineering: Functions are the primary unit of decomposition; clean signatures with clear returns make code easier to test, reuse, and reason about.
whyItMatters.scalability: First-class functions enable composition patterns — middleware, handlers, pipelines — that let large systems grow without rewriting core logic.
whyItMatters.cost: Catching errors at the call site instead of via expensive stack-unwinding exceptions keeps the hot path cheap and predictable.
whyItMatters.reliability: The `(value, error)` convention forces callers to acknowledge failure paths, which is a major reason idiomatic Go services degrade gracefully instead of crashing.

coreComponents.name: Function signature
coreComponents.definition: The `func name(params) (results)` declaration specifying parameter types and return types.
coreComponents.purpose: Define the contract between caller and callee.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Declare parameter names/types, return arity and types, and the function name.

coreComponents.name: Multiple return values
coreComponents.definition: A function may return more than one value, written as a parenthesized type list.
coreComponents.purpose: Return a result and metadata (commonly an error) together without containers or globals.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Produce every declared return value on each `return` path.
coreComponents.examples: return q, nil  // value and error

coreComponents.name: Named return values
coreComponents.definition: Result parameters given names in the signature, pre-initialized to their zero values.
coreComponents.purpose: Document intent, enable naked returns, and let `defer` inspect/modify the result.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Act as ordinary local variables that are returned when `return` runs.

coreComponents.name: Variadic parameter
coreComponents.definition: A final parameter written `...T` that accepts any number of arguments as a slice.
coreComponents.purpose: Allow flexible call sites like fmt.Println without manual slice construction.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Collect trailing arguments into a `[]T`; callers may spread a slice with `s...`.

coreComponents.name: Function value / closure
coreComponents.definition: A function used as a value, optionally capturing variables from its enclosing scope.
coreComponents.purpose: Enable higher-order functions, callbacks, and stateful generators.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Carry a code pointer plus references to captured variables.

internalWorking: When a function is called, Go evaluates the arguments left to right and passes them by value — a copy is made (for slices/maps/pointers the copied value is the header/pointer, not the underlying data).
Return values are placed into result slots; with multiple returns the callee writes each result, and the caller reads the whole tuple in one assignment.
Named return values are allocated and zero-initialized at function entry, behaving as ordinary locals that the `return` statement (or a naked `return`) hands back.

A variadic `...T` parameter is implemented as a `[]T`; when called with individual args Go allocates a fresh slice, and when called with `slice...` it passes the existing slice header directly (no copy of elements).

`defer` statements are pushed onto a per-goroutine stack and run LIFO after `return` assigns the result values but before control returns to the caller — so a deferred closure can read and mutate named return values.
A closure is represented as a pointer to a function plus a pointer to the captured variables (heap-allocated if they escape), which is why closures share and observe later changes to those variables.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: caller --evaluate args (by value)--> [push frame, init named returns to zero] --> run body --> return assigns result slots --> [deferred funcs run LIFO, may mutate named returns] --> result tuple handed back to caller
dataFlowWalkthrough: The caller writes `q, err := div(10, 2)`, so Go evaluates 10 and 2 and copies them into div's parameters a and b.
Inside div, the body checks b and either returns `(0, errors.New(...))` or `(a/b, nil)`, writing both result slots.
If div has a deferred function, it executes after the return values are set, potentially adjusting a named error before the caller sees it.
Control returns and the caller binds q to the first result and err to the second in one assignment.
The caller inspects err first (`if err != nil`) and only trusts q when err is nil — the canonical Go usage pattern.

keyTerminology.meaning: A function returning more than one value, e.g., `(int, error)`.
keyTerminology.importance: The backbone of Go error handling and many stdlib APIs.

keyTerminology.meaning: A bare `return` in a function with named results, returning their current values.
keyTerminology.importance: Concise but can hurt readability in long functions; a common interview gotcha.

keyTerminology.meaning: A function whose last parameter `...T` accepts any number of arguments.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables flexible APIs; understanding slice spreading (`s...`) is key.

keyTerminology.meaning: A function value that captures and references variables from its enclosing scope.
keyTerminology.importance: Powers callbacks, generators, and middleware — and a source of capture bugs.

keyTerminology.meaning: A placeholder that discards an unwanted return value.
keyTerminology.importance: Lets you ignore one result (e.g., the value) while keeping the other (e.g., error).

importantConcepts.explanation: Go does not throw; functions return an `error` as an ordinary value. The caller checks `if err != nil` and decides what to do, making control flow explicit and local.
Go copies arguments. For large structs that means a copy cost; for slices/maps/pointers the small header/pointer is copied so the callee can mutate the shared underlying data.

Because named return values are real variables, a deferred closure can read them (e.g., for logging) or reassign them (e.g., to wrap an error with context), and that change is what the caller receives.

variationsAndTypes: Single-return functions (a pure transformation like `func double(x int) int`).
Multi-return functions, especially the `(T, error)` and comma-ok `(value, bool)` forms.
Named-return functions enabling naked returns and defer-based result mutation.
Variadic functions for flexible argument counts (fmt.Printf, append-style helpers).
Higher-order functions and closures that take or return other functions.
advantages: Multiple returns make success and failure explicit at every call site, improving reliability.
No exception machinery means predictable, cheap control flow on the happy path.
First-class functions and closures enable powerful composition (middleware, callbacks, pipelines).
Variadic functions provide ergonomic, flexible APIs without overloading.
Named returns plus defer allow clean, centralized error wrapping and resource cleanup.
disadvantages: Repetitive `if err != nil` boilerplate at nearly every call site.
Naked returns can obscure what is actually returned in long functions.
Closures capturing variables by reference can introduce subtle bugs (shared/mutated state).
Passing large structs by value can be an unintended performance cost.
It is easy to ignore a returned error with `_` and silently swallow failures.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use multiple returns for any operation that can fail (return `(T, error)`), use named returns when defer must touch the result or names clarify a short function, and use variadics for genuinely variable argument counts.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid naked returns in long functions, avoid named returns purely to save typing, and avoid variadics when a clear fixed signature or a slice parameter is more honest about intent.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A function is like a vending machine: you insert inputs (money + selection) and it returns two things at once — your snack and your change, or your snack and an 'out of stock' light (the error). You always check the light before trusting the tray. A variadic machine is one where you can press as many buttons as you like in one go, and a closure is a machine that remembers how many snacks it has already dispensed today.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go uses exceptions like Java or Python.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go returns errors as values; `panic`/`recover` exist but are for truly exceptional, unrecoverable situations, not normal error flow.
It returns the current values of the named result variables, which were zero-initialized at entry and may have been assigned in the body or by a defer.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Passing a slice to a variadic function copies all the elements.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Calling with `s...` passes the existing slice header, so no element copy occurs and mutations to the underlying array are shared.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Closures capture the value of a variable at the time they are created.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Closures capture the variable itself by reference, so they observe later changes — the classic loop-capture footgun before Go 1.22.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Lean function signatures and value semantics keep call paths predictable; avoid passing huge structs by value on hot paths to reduce copy and GC pressure.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Always return and check errors; wrap them with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` so failures carry context across layers.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Use deferred cleanup (file/connection close, mutex unlock) so functions release resources even on error or panic paths.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Instrument function boundaries that can fail with metrics/spans so error rates and latencies per operation are observable.
productionConsiderations.security: Never silently discard an error with `_` for security-relevant operations (auth checks, crypto, validation); a swallowed error can mean an unchecked failure.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Prefer pointer receivers/parameters for large structs to avoid copy cost, and reuse closures rather than recreating heavy captured state per call.
productionConsiderations.performance: Be aware that closures capturing variables may force heap allocation (escape analysis); profile with `go build -gcflags=-m` and pprof when allocation matters.

codeExamples.title: Multiple return values and the (T, error) idiom
codeExamples.overview: A division function that returns both a result and an error, plus the canonical caller check using the blank identifier where appropriate.
codeExamples.breakdown: div declares two return types `(int, error)`. On the failure path it returns a zero result and a non-nil error; on success it returns the quotient and nil. The caller binds both with `q, err := div(...)` and checks `err != nil` first. The second call uses the blank identifier `_` to ignore the numeric result because only the error matters there.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using the value before checking the error, or ignoring the error entirely with `_`, which hides failures.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Return a sentinel like `var ErrDivZero = errors.New(...)` so callers can compare with errors.Is, instead of allocating a fresh error string every call.

codeExamples.title: Named return values, naked return, and defer mutating the result
codeExamples.overview: Show named results enabling a naked return and a deferred closure that wraps the returned error with context.
codeExamples.breakdown: split names its results `(x, y int)`; they start at zero and are assigned in the body, then `return` with no operands sends them back. parse names `(n int, err error)` and registers a deferred closure that runs after `return` sets err but before the caller receives it — so it can wrap err with `%w`. This is the idiomatic way to add context to all error paths in one place.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using naked returns in long functions hurts readability; forgetting that defer only mutates NAMED returns (it cannot change unnamed ones).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Reserve named returns for short functions or for the defer-based error-wrapping pattern; otherwise prefer explicit returns for clarity.

codeExamples.title: Variadic functions and spreading a slice
codeExamples.overview: A sum function that accepts any number of ints, called both with literals and by spreading an existing slice.
codeExamples.breakdown: The `nums ...int` parameter must be last; inside the function it is an ordinary `[]int`. Calling `sum(1, 2, 3)` makes Go allocate a slice of those args. Calling `sum()` yields a nil slice (len 0). Calling `sum(values...)` spreads the existing slice header in directly, avoiding a copy of the elements.
codeExamples.commonIssues: You cannot mix spread and individual args in one call (`sum(1, values...)` is a compile error); the variadic param must be the final parameter.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you already hold a slice, spreading with `s...` avoids the allocation that passing individual args would cause.

codeExamples.title: First-class functions and closures
codeExamples.overview: Functions as values: a closure-based counter that captures state, and a higher-order function that takes a function argument.
codeExamples.breakdown: makeCounter returns an anonymous function (type `func() int`) that closes over `count`; because the closure captures the variable by reference, each call increments the same `count`, so successive calls yield 1, 2, 3. apply shows functions as parameters: it accepts any `func(int) int` and applies it elementwise. Passing a function literal inline is the everyday higher-order pattern.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Two separate calls to makeCounter produce independent counters; assuming closures copy the captured value (they share it) leads to surprises, as does capturing a loop variable before Go 1.22.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Closures capturing variables may escape to the heap; if a hot loop allocates closures repeatedly, hoist the function or avoid capture to cut GC pressure.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A payments service must parse incoming amount strings, validate them, apply a percentage fee, and report precise, contextual errors so failed transactions can be diagnosed without crashing the request handler.
endToEndExample.inputData: A list of raw amount strings such as ["100", "49.99", "", "abc"] and a fee rate of 2.5%.
endToEndExample.architecture: A small pipeline of pure-ish functions: parseAmount returns `(float64, error)`; applyFee is a higher-order function that returns a closure capturing the rate; a variadic logf helper formats messages; and the orchestrator uses named returns with a deferred error-wrapper.
processingSteps: parseAmount(s) returns the parsed float plus an error using the (T, error) idiom.
A deferred closure in the orchestrator wraps any returned error with the offending input via %w.
applyFee(rate) returns a closure (func(float64) float64) that captures rate and computes amount*(1+rate).
Iterate the inputs, skip and log invalid ones using a variadic logf, accumulate valid totals.
Return the final total and a nil error, or zero and a wrapped error on the first hard failure.
endToEndExample.output: Valid amounts are summed with fees applied; invalid entries are logged with context, and the function returns a total plus a nil/non-nil error.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Emit a counter for parse failures per input and a histogram of processed-batch sizes; alert if the failure ratio exceeds a threshold.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Each parse uses (value, error); the orchestrator's deferred closure wraps errors with the input string so logs pinpoint the bad record, and the blank identifier is never used on the parse error.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The batch ["100","49.99","","abc"] yields a total over the two valid amounts with a 2.5% fee, two logged-and-skipped invalid records, and a clear wrapped error only if a hard-stop condition is configured — demonstrating multi-return, named returns + defer, variadics, and closures working together.

industryUseCases.problem: Thousands of internal services need consistent, explicit error propagation in Go.
industryUseCases.solution: Pervasive use of the `(T, error)` idiom plus error wrapping with %w so failures carry context across call layers.
industryUseCases.benefits: Failures are visible and traceable at every boundary, reducing silent data corruption and easing debugging.

industryUseCases.problem: Tools like Terraform expose flexible APIs and configurable behaviors.
industryUseCases.solution: Functional options pattern — variadic `...Option` functions (closures) that mutate a config struct.
industryUseCases.benefits: Backward-compatible, self-documenting constructors that grow without breaking existing call sites.

industryUseCases.problem: HTTP servers must layer cross-cutting concerns like auth, logging, and recovery.
industryUseCases.solution: Middleware built from higher-order functions that take and return `http.Handler` closures.
industryUseCases.benefits: Composable request pipelines where each concern is an independently testable function.

industryUseCases.problem: Many operations can partially fail and must report precise reasons.
industryUseCases.solution: Functions returning `(result, error)` with sentinel errors checked via errors.Is/As across the codebase.
industryUseCases.benefits: Callers can branch on specific failure kinds and surface actionable status to operators.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Keep signatures small and avoid passing large structs by value on hot paths; use pointers or accept interfaces so functions compose without copy overhead as call volume grows.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Pair every resource acquisition with `defer` cleanup (Close/Unlock) so functions release resources on every return path, including error and panic paths.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Wrap errors with context (%w) and propagate them up rather than panicking, so a single bad request degrades gracefully instead of taking down the process.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Design functions to be idempotent where possible so retried calls after a failure do not double-apply side effects.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use escape analysis (`go build -gcflags=-m`) to see when closures and named returns force heap allocation; hoist closures out of hot loops to reduce GC churn.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Prefer pointer parameters/receivers for large data to avoid copies; reuse closures with captured state instead of recreating them per request.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Never discard errors from security-relevant functions (auth, crypto, input validation) with the blank identifier; an unchecked error can mean an unverified operation succeeded silently.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Instrument fallible function boundaries with spans/metrics keyed by operation name so error rates and latencies are attributable to specific functions.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Return explicit validation errors from parsing/transform functions rather than coercing bad input to zero values, so invalid data is rejected at the boundary.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Use the deferred-named-return pattern to attach the failing input/context to errors, then log the wrapped error with a request/trace ID and alert on elevated failure ratios.

recommendedPractices: Return errors as the last value and check `if err != nil` immediately at the call site.
Wrap errors with `fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)` to preserve the chain for errors.Is/As.
Use the blank identifier `_` only when you genuinely do not need a return value.
Use `defer` for cleanup right after acquiring a resource so the release is co-located.
Pass functions/closures for cross-cutting behavior (callbacks, middleware, options).
engineeringStandards: Run `go vet` and a linter (e.g., errcheck) in CI to catch unchecked errors.
Keep functions small and single-purpose; long functions with naked returns are a smell.
Prefer explicit returns over naked returns except for the defer-error-wrapping idiom.
designRecommendations: Make the (T, error) order consistent: value(s) first, error last.
Use the functional-options pattern (variadic `...Option`) for constructors with many optional settings.
Spread an existing slice with `s...` into variadic calls instead of rebuilding arguments.
namingConventions: Name functions as verbs describing the action (parseAmount, fetchUser), not nouns.
Name the error result `err` and value results meaningfully when using named returns.
Prefix sentinel error variables with `Err` (ErrNotFound) per convention.
documentationStandards: Document the meaning of each return value, especially when a non-nil value may accompany a non-nil error.
State the error conditions a function can return in its doc comment.
Note any side effects a closure-capturing function has on captured state.
testingStrategies: Table-driven tests covering both the success and error return paths of each function.
Assert wrapped errors with errors.Is/errors.As rather than string matching.
Test variadic functions with zero, one, many, and spread-slice argument forms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a returned value before checking the error.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Habit from exception-based languages where success is assumed.
commonMistakes.impact: Operating on a zero/invalid value, causing wrong results or downstream panics.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always check `if err != nil` and return/handle before touching the value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swallowing errors with the blank identifier (`v, _ := f()`).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Treating the error as noise to make the code compile quickly.
commonMistakes.impact: Silent failures that surface much later as data corruption or outages.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Handle, log, or propagate the error; only use `_` when failure is truly irrelevant.

commonMistakes.mistake: Overusing naked returns in long functions.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Convenience of not retyping the result variables.
commonMistakes.impact: Readers cannot tell what is returned, hiding bugs where a result was never set.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use explicit returns; reserve naked returns for very short functions or the defer pattern.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting `defer` to modify an unnamed return value.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming defer can change any result, not just named ones.
commonMistakes.impact: The deferred mutation is silently ignored, so error wrapping never takes effect.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use named return values when a deferred closure must read or change the result.

commonMistakes.mistake: Capturing a loop variable in a closure (pre-Go 1.22).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Closures capture the variable by reference, and the loop variable was shared.
commonMistakes.impact: All closures observe the final loop value, producing wrong results.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: On Go <1.22 shadow the variable (`v := v`) or pass it as an argument; Go 1.22+ scopes it per iteration.

comparisonSection.explanation: Go makes failure an explicit value the caller must handle locally; exceptions propagate implicitly and can be forgotten, but reduce boilerplate.
Multiple returns are clearer and avoid mutating caller state; out-params (C-style) work but obscure the data flow and require pre-allocated storage.
Named returns document intent and enable defer-based mutation but can encourage hard-to-read naked returns; unnamed returns force explicit, clear `return` statements.
Pointers avoid copying large structs and allow mutation; values are safer and simpler but copy the whole struct on each call.

beginnerQuestions.question: How does a Go function return multiple values, and what is the common idiom?
beginnerQuestions.answer: List multiple types in parentheses, e.g., `func div(a, b int) (int, error)`; the idiomatic pair is `(result, error)`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests the foundational Go convention for results and error handling.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does the blank identifier `_` do in a multi-return assignment?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It discards a return value you do not need, e.g., `_, err := f()` keeps only the error.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Checks understanding of selectively ignoring results without unused-variable errors.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a variadic function and how do you call one with a slice?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A function with a final `...T` parameter that takes any number of args; pass a slice by spreading it with `slice...`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests knowledge of flexible argument lists and slice spreading.

intermediateQuestions.question: What are named return values and what is a naked return?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Named results are result parameters named in the signature, zero-initialized at entry; a naked `return` (no operands) sends back their current values.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Probes a subtle Go feature that affects readability and defer behavior.

intermediateQuestions.question: How can a deferred function modify what a function returns?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Only when the function uses named return values; the deferred closure runs after return sets them and can reassign, e.g., to wrap an error.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests the interaction between defer and named returns, a common gotcha.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why are Go functions called first-class, and what is a closure?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Functions can be assigned, passed, and returned like any value; a closure is a function value that captures variables from its enclosing scope by reference.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Checks understanding of higher-order functions and variable capture.

advancedQuestions.question: Are arguments passed by value or reference in Go, and why can a function still mutate a caller's slice?
advancedQuestions.answer: Everything is passed by value, but a slice value is a header (pointer, len, cap); copying the header still points at the same backing array, so element mutations are visible to the caller.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests deep understanding of Go's value semantics versus reference-like types.

advancedQuestions.question: When does a closure cause heap allocation, and how would you detect it?
advancedQuestions.answer: When captured variables escape the function's stack frame (they outlive the call), escape analysis moves them to the heap; detect with `go build -gcflags=-m`.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Probes performance awareness around closures and escape analysis.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the loop-variable capture bug and what Go 1.22 changed.
advancedQuestions.answer: Pre-1.22 the loop variable was shared, so closures captured the same variable and saw the final value; Go 1.22 makes the loop variable per-iteration, fixing the common bug.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests up-to-date language knowledge and closure semantics.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A function returns `(*User, error)` and a caller dereferences the user even when err is non-nil, causing nil-pointer panics in production.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: On the error path the value is often nil/zero; the caller must check err before using the value. The contract should state whether a non-nil value can accompany an error.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Enforce checking `if err != nil` first and returning early; document the value-on-error semantics; add a lint rule (errcheck) and table tests covering the error path.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a configurable HTTP client constructor in Go that supports many optional settings without breaking existing callers as options grow.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use the functional-options pattern: `New(opts ...Option)` where each Option is a closure `func(*config)` that mutates a config struct; defaults are set first, then options applied in order.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: More flexible and backward-compatible than a giant parameter list or config struct, but slightly more indirection and harder for newcomers to discover all options.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Adding a new setting is a new `WithX` option function with no signature change, so the API scales without breaking the thousands of existing call sites.

followUpQuestions: How would you wrap and later inspect errors using %w, errors.Is, and errors.As?
When is a value return (no error) acceptable for an operation that could fail?
How do you decide between a variadic parameter and a slice parameter?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A Go function is a first-class value that can take multiple typed parameters and return multiple typed results, with the `(value, error)` pair as the idiomatic failure convention.
keyConcepts: Multiple returns: `func f() (int, error)`; check the error first.
Named returns enable naked `return` and defer-based result mutation.
Variadic: `func f(xs ...int)`; spread a slice with `s...`.
Functions are values; closures capture variables by reference.
Blank identifier `_` discards an unwanted return value.
formulas: Defer can mutate result  <=>  the result is a NAMED return value
commands: go build -gcflags=-m ./...   # see escape analysis / heap allocations
go test -run TestX -v        # exercise success and error return paths
interviewPoints: Errors are values, returned not thrown.
Pass-by-value always; slices/maps copy the header, not the data.
`sum(s...)` spreads a slice; variadic param must be last.
quickNotes: Naked returns hurt readability in long functions.
Closures share captured variables; pre-1.22 loop capture is a footgun.
Wrap errors with %w to keep the chain for errors.Is/As.

keyTakeaways: Go functions return multiple values, and the `(result, error)` idiom makes failure an explicit value the caller must handle — there are no exceptions for normal error flow.
Named return values (zero-initialized at entry) enable naked returns and, crucially, let a deferred closure read or wrap the returned error before the caller sees it.
Variadic functions (`...T`) accept any number of arguments as a slice, and you spread an existing slice into them with `s...` without copying elements.

Functions are first-class values: closures capture surrounding variables by reference, powering callbacks, middleware, and the functional-options pattern — but watch for capture and escape-allocation pitfalls.
